reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Rose and Alaya found a small house in the forest. It was made of sticks and old plastic bags. "Let's play house here," said Alaya. "Yes!" said Rose.

They set out leaves for plates. They set out pinecones for babies. Rose picked up a pinecone. "I am the parent," said Rose. "I feed the baby." "No, I am the parent," said Alaya. "I want to feed the baby too."

Both girls wanted to be the parent. Both girls stood still. The baby pinecone sat on the ground. Nobody fed it. Mr. Nasser, their neighbour, was walking by with his dog. He stopped and smiled. "You can both be the parent," he said. "Just not at the same time. One of you can be the baby, and then you can switch halfway."

"Alaya first," said Rose. "Then me." Alaya held the pinecone. She rocked it and sang. "Baby, baby, time to eat." Rose got down on her knees. She was the baby now. She drank pretend soup from a leaf. "More, please," said Rose. Alaya laughed and filled the leaf again.

Then they switched. Rose was the parent now. She held the pinecone up high. "Time for a hug, baby!" Alaya was the baby. She yawned a big yawn. "Sleepy, sleepy," said Alaya. Rose patted her back, very soft.

They played all afternoon. Parent, then baby. Baby, then parent. "Best house ever," said Rose. Alaya hugged the pinecone tight and said, "See you tomorrow, baby."

story:

Ms. Cho put something in Arnaud's hands. It was small and heavy. He touched it with his fingertips. His fingertips felt it all over. Smooth. Very smooth. "A stone!" he said. "Yes," said Ms. Cho. She gave him a new thing. His fingertips felt little bumps everywhere. Bumpy, bumpy, bumpy. "A pinecone!" he said. Jay clapped.

Then Arnaud held something light. His fingertips said soft, like a tickle. He smelled it too. It smelled like nothing much. He touched it again, soft and smooth. "A feather," he said. Ms. Cho took off the string. There it was, a white feather. Arnaud touched it one more time with his fingertips. "Soft," he said.

story:
Rosalie went to the store with her dad. Evaan and Crew were there too. They saw a big box of toy bears near the door. One bear had soft brown fur. Rosalie wanted that bear so much.

Rosalie grabbed the brown bear fast. But Evaan was holding it first. Evaan's face went sad. He started to cry. Rosalie heard him sniffle. Her tummy felt funny and tight. She did not want that.

Then Rosalie remembered. She put the bear back in Evaan's hands. "Can I have a turn, please?" she asked. "When you are done?" Evaan wiped his eyes. "Yes," he said. "You asked. Okay." He hugged the bear once. Then he gave it to Rosalie.

Rosalie held the soft brown bear. "Your turn now," she said after a bit. She gave it back. Evaan smiled big. Crew clapped his hands. Dad came close and smiled too. "Time to go," he said. Rosalie waved to Evaan and Crew. "Bye, bear," she said. "Bye, friends."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Elizabeth wanted to make muffins for her family. Her mom said, "Yes, let's cook in the backyard." They set a little table by the friendly oak tree.

Elizabeth grabbed the sugar bag. She poured it straight into the bowl. Sugar went everywhere. Too much sugar sat in a big hill. "Oops," said Elizabeth. Her back felt sticky.

Mom held up a small cup. "This is a measuring cup," she said. Elizabeth scooped sugar with it. She filled it up and tapped it flat. Then she used a measuring spoon for the vanilla. Just the right little bit went in. Not too much. Not too little. The batter looked smooth and good.

Mom put the pan in the hot oven. Elizabeth watched from her chair, far away and safe. Soon the muffins were done. The family sat on the grass to eat. "Yum," said Dad. Elizabeth caught a crumb in her hand and smiled. "I made these," she said.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Connor woke up and looked out the window. "Snow!" he said. The grass was gone. White snow was everywhere. No school today! It was a snow day at home.

Connor put on his boots and his coat. He ran out the door to play. But the sidewalk was icy. His feet went slip, slip, slip! Down he went, right on his bottom. "Oof," said Connor.

His dad came out too. Dad did not run. Dad took small, slow steps. His feet went tap, tap, tap. "Watch me," said Dad. Connor stood up. He took small, slow steps too. Tap, tap, tap. His feet did not slip! "I did it!" said Connor.

Connor stomped in the soft snow. The snow was bumpy in some spots. He found a surprise under a bush. Little bird tracks, like tiny stamps! "Who made these?" Connor wondered. He followed them, slow and careful, tap, tap, tap, all the way to the fence.

story:

They both held the horse. It did not rock at all. Claire looked at Lyana. Lyana looked at Claire. "We can take turns," said Lyana. "You go first, one after another. Then me." Claire nodded.

Claire climbed on. She rocked and rocked. The horse went squeak, squeak. "Silly horse," said Claire, and she laughed. Lyana counted to ten. Then Claire got off. Now it was Lyana's go. Lyana rocked fast, and her hair flew up. Claire waited. She tapped her toes on the grass-green rug. It was hard to wait. But then Lyana got off, and Claire got another go.

Ms. Choi came over with two scarves. She tied a red scarf on the horse. "It looks like a knight's horse now," said Ms. Choi. Claire gasped. A surprise! Lyana rode the silly knight horse first. Then Claire rode it after her. One go, then another go, all the way to snack time. "My turn again?" asked Claire. "Yes," said Lyana. "After me!"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Raphael ran to Manuel at daycare. "Can I come to your house now?" he asked. "I want to see your beach ball."

Manuel smiled. "Not now," he said. "We go after a sleep. Tomorrow."

Raphael frowned. "What is tomorrow?"

Ms. Toussaint knelt down beside them. "Tomorrow comes after today," she said.

"But I want to go now," said Raphael.

"Now we play here," said Manuel. "Then we sleep. Then it is tomorrow."

Raphael looked out the window. The sun was up. Today was now.

After school, Raphael ate his snack. Then he slept in his bed. When he woke up, the sun was up again. "Is it tomorrow?" he asked his dad.

"Yes," his dad said, smiling. "Today is the new day."

At Manuel's house, they threw the beach ball high. Raphael held up his drawing with the sharp point of his pencil.

"I waited, and now it is today!" he said.

story:
Austin stood by the lemon tree in his backyard. His eyes saw four yellow lemons on a branch. His ears heard a bee buzz by. His nose smelled something sharp and fresh. "Lemons," said his dad. "They are ready to pick."

Austin wanted lemonade. He thought lemons would taste like orange juice, sweet and yummy. His dad picked one lemon and cut a thin slice. Austin put the slice in his mouth. His tongue tingled. His whole face scrunched up. "Sour!" he said. "So sour!"

His friend Evan came over with a big grin. "You made a sour face," Evan said. Austin laughed and gave Evan a tiny taste. Evan's face scrunched up too. Then the boys touched the lemon skin. It was bumpy and cool.

Dad squeezed the lemons into a jug. He added water and sugar. Austin stirred it with a long spoon. The juice and the sugar sank and swirled together. They drank cold cups in the shade. Austin took a sip and smiled big. "Sweet now!" he said. "And a little bit sour too."

story:
Gabriel sat in his car seat. Dad was driving to the park. Gabriel had a little bag of grapes.

"You can have three grapes," said Dad. "Not more."

Gabriel looked at his grapes. Some were small. Some were big. Did big grapes count as more?

"Is a big grape still one?" he asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "Three means three grapes. Big or small."

Gabriel picked three big grapes. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three." Then he ate them, one by one.

He heard rain tap the roof. One tap, then more taps. The rain made a song. Dad sang, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

A grape fell from Gabriel's hand. It rolled under the seat. He could not reach it.

"I will pay attention and hold on tight," Gabriel said. He held the next grape with both hands.

The rain stopped. The sky looked beautiful and blue.

"We are here," said Dad. He helped Gabriel out of the car. They held hands and walked to the swings.

"Can I have three grapes later?" asked Gabriel.

"Yes," said Dad. "Three is three, every time."

Gabriel smiled. He swung his arms and counted the swings. "One, two, three!"

story:
Eliana wanted to zip her own coat. But the zipper was stuck at the bottom. She pulled and pulled. It did not move.

She called her dad. "Count while you pull," he said. "One, two..." Then Eliana forgot what came next. She stood very still.

Then she remembered a song. "One, two, buckle my shoe," she sang. "Three, four, shut the door." Dad smiled and clapped the beat. The words rhymed, so they came out easy. "Five, six, pick up sticks." On "pick," she grabbed the zipper tab with her fingers. "Seven, eight, lay them straight." The zipper slid up, up, up. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen!" The coat was zipped all the way to her chin.

Eliana picked up her red hat. "I did it with my song," she said. Dad gave her a real hug. "Sing it at school for Krew," he said. Eliana ran to the door. "One, two, buckle my shoe!" she sang.

story:

story:
Arnaud loved the big red blocks at school. Today he got to the block corner first. He stacked one, then two, then three. The tower grew tall.

Hallie and Matheo came over. "Can we play too?" Hallie asked. Arnaud looked at his tower. "These are my blocks," he said. "All of them?" Matheo asked. "All of them," said Arnaud.

Hallie walked away. Matheo walked away. Arnaud built alone. The room felt quiet. He looked at Hallie. She was drawing with her finger in the air. He looked at Matheo. He was spinning in a circle. Nobody was building.

Arnaud pushed the blocks into one big pile. Then he stopped. What if he made three piles? He counted them out. "Hallie! Matheo!" he called. "Look. One pile for me. One pile for you. One pile for you."

Hallie ran back fast. Matheo ran back fast too. Each child built a small tower. "Can I put my block on top of yours?" Arnaud asked. "Yes," said Hallie. "You say please, that's polite." "Please," said Arnaud.

The three towers stood side by side in a row. Matheo clapped his hands. Hallie moved her tower closer so they touched. Arnaud grinned and said, "Blocks for everyone."

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Miles sat at the table. Mom put down a big pot. It smelled warm, like rice and peas.

"Tonight we say the blessing first," said Mom. "It is special. We fold our hands."

Miles wanted to eat right now. The rice smelled so good. But Mom said, "Watch Grandpa."

Grandpa bowed his head. He closed his eyes. Miles peeked. He saw Grandpa's eyes shut and Grandpa's head down. Miles closed his eyes too. He bowed his head. "Thank you for our food," he said, in his little voice.

Then Miles opened one eye. Grandpa was still bowing. Miles closed his eye fast. He waited. The room was very quiet. He could hear the pot steam going tss, tss.

"Amen," said Grandpa. Everyone said "Amen." Mom smiled big. "Miles said it with us!"

Miles clapped. The blessing was done, and now it was time to eat. Miles took his spoon. "I did it!" he said. "Can we say it again tomorrow?"

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
story:
Eleanor went to the corner store with her dad. Apples sat in a big box. "Can I count them?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. Eleanor pointed at the apples. "One, two, three, four, five, six." But she pointed at one apple two times. "Six!" she said. Dad shook his head. "Count again," he said. "Point to each apple one time."

Eleanor tried again. She tapped one apple and said one number. "One, two, three, four, five." Five apples! She had said one number for each apple. She jumped up and down. "Five apples!"

Next, Eleanor looked at two little piles of pears. She counted the first pile. Four pears. She counted the second pile. Seven pears. "This pile has more!" she said, pointing. Mr. Korhonen, the store man, smiled. He put one pear in the middle of the small pile. "Now count again," he said. Eleanor tapped each pear one time. "Five!" she said. Still not more than seven. She giggled and gave the pear back.

At home, Eleanor counted her toy cars. One car got two taps by mistake. She lifted her finger and started over. "One, two, three, four." She ran to Dad with all four cars. "I counted just right!" she said. "Can we go back tomorrow?"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Harper wanted to bake cookies with Dad. She asked, "Can we bake now?"

"Not now," said Dad. "We will bake later."

Harper frowned. "Is it later yet?" she asked.

"No, not yet," said Dad.

Harper followed Dad to the laundry room. He put a shirt in the washer. Then he put a towel in. "One shirt, one towel," he said.

"Is it later yet?" asked Harper.

"Not yet," said Dad. "Later means some time after now, not right away."

Harper waited. She counted the socks. "One sock, two socks, three socks."

The washer went swish, swish. Then it stopped.

"Now is it later?" she asked.

Dad smiled. "Yes! Now it is later."

They washed their hands. Harper helped pour the sugar. She was careful and stood back from the hot oven. Dad put the cookies in.

"One cookie, two cookies, three cookies," said Harper.

"Tomorrow we can bake more," said Dad.

"Tomorrow!" said Harper. "I love tomorrow."

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
The bookmobile stopped on Myles' street. Myles ran up the steps with his dad. Mr. Mansour smiled and handed him a card. "Your very first library card," he said. Myles held it with both hands.

Myles picked a book about tools. There was a hammer on the cover. He read it in the corner. Then he slid it onto a shelf by the door.

"Wait," said Mr. Mansour. "See that little white label on the spine? That label shows where the book belongs." Myles looked at the letters. He pulled the book out and matched the label to the shelf. It slid right into its spot.

"Did the label do that?" Myles asked. His dad nodded. "It did."

Then the bookmobile began to beep. "Time to go," Mr. Mansour spoke softly. "Take your book home. Bring it back soon."

Myles carried the hammer book down the steps. He held his card up high.

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Madelyn sat in the family car. Her tummy felt jumpy. Today she would get a shot at the doctor.

"I think the needle is big," said Madelyn. "Big like a boat!"

"Say what you see at the doctor," said Mom. "Then we will come back to the car."

At the doctor, Madelyn held her bear tight. The doctor held up a thin, thin needle. "One quick poke," said the doctor. "Ready?"

Poke. Done. Madelyn blinked. "It was tiny! Not big like a boat. Just a quick poke in my arm." She looked at her arm. A small bandage sat there like a little white boat.

"That was so fast!" said Madelyn.

"Very fast," said Mom. "You did it."

Back in the car, Madelyn grinned. "Shots are just a quick poke with a thin needle. That is all!" She waved her bandage out the window. "Can we get a tasty snack now?"

"Yes," said Mom, starting the car. "You earned it."

Madelyn hugged her bear. "Quick poke, thin needle, all done!"

"Home we go," said Mom, and the car rolled down the road.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Aurora sat in the family car. She was going to the dentist. It was her first time. She held her little bag on her lap. Inside was her toothbrush, ready to show.

"One toothbrush, one girl," said Aurora. She liked that.

Mommy started the car. Aurora peeked in her bag. She saw a toothbrush. But it was blue. Her toothbrush was green. This one was not hers. It was the baby's toothbrush. "Not mine, not mine," said Aurora.

Mommy looked in the mirror. "The baby uses that one," she said. "Each person uses their own toothbrush." Then the car went on. Aurora held the blue toothbrush. She did not use it. She just looked at it.

At the dentist, Aurora opened wide. The dentist counted her teeth. One, two, three, up to twenty. Then Aurora smiled a big smile. "No bad teeth today," said the dentist. "Good brushing!"

Back in the car, Aurora held her bag tight. At home, she ran to the bathroom. She put the blue toothbrush back by the baby's cup. She took her own green one. "One toothbrush, one girl," said Aurora. She gave it a big hug.

story:
Eleanor ran to the kitchen with muddy hands. "Soup time!" she called.

Her dad pointed to the sink. "We wash our hands before we eat," he said.

Eleanor looked at her hands. They were brown. "My hands are wearing mud shirts!" she said. Her dad laughed.

She went to the sink. He turned on the water. It was warm, not hot. Eleanor rubbed her hands together. The mud went down the drain. Now her hands were pink and clean.

Back at the table, there was soup and bread. Eleanor dipped the bread in. "Salty!" she said, and made a funny face. "Salty soup, clean hands."

Her dad held up his own hands. "Wash first, eat after," he said, and winked. Eleanor giggled and took another big bite.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Brooks was in the playroom. The sun made a warm spot on the rug. His friend Dexter was there too.

"Let's put things in piles," said Dexter. "Animals here. Toys here. Food here."

Brooks picked up a cow. It went in the animal pile. He picked up a banana. It went in the food pile. He picked up a little red car. It went in the toy pile.

Then Brooks found a soft brown dog. He put it in the animal pile. Dexter shook his head. "That is a toy," he said. "It is not alive."

Brooks looked at the dog. It did not bark. It did not wag. It just sat there, soft and quiet.

The real dog at home barked. This one did not. Brooks picked it up. He put it in the toy pile, next to the red car.

"Now it is not lost," said Brooks.

"Wait," said Dexter. "The food pile is empty."

Brooks smiled. He ran to the toy kitchen. He came back with a apple, a carrot, and a egg. They went in the food pile, one by one.

Mr. Jung looked in the door. "Nice tidy piles," he said.

The soft brown dog sat with the toys. It was quiet. It was not alive. It was right where it belonged.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Declan sat in his car seat. He was going home from the park with his dad. His tummy rumbled. He wanted a warm bath and his pillow right after.

"Big bath tonight," said Dad. "You got very muddy."

Declan smiled. At home, Dad turned on the water. Declan wanted to jump in. He stopped. "Wait," he said. "You check first."

Dad put his hand in the water. "Too hot," he said. "Watch this."

Dad turned the tap. Cold water ran in. Steam went up, then it stopped. Dad checked the water again. "Now it is warm," he said.

Declan put in his toes. Warm, not hot. He slid in all the way.

Declan had an idea. "Does the tap make cold water too?" he asked.

Dad showed him. Declan put his hand near the cold tap. Brrr. He pulled back fast.

"So taps can be hot or cold," said Declan. "And you check first."

"Check first," said Dad. "Every time."

Declan splashed and played. His rubber duck floated past his knee. Then he hugged his towel, warm and soft like a big pillow. "Bath time is the best," he said. "After you check first."

story:

Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya held up her hand. "Let's count the chairs," she said. "One, two, three, four, five." Then Francesca counted too. "One, two, three, four, six." She frowned. "That sounds funny."

Jaxson listened hard. "Six comes after five," he said. Francesca tried again. "One, two, three, four, five, six." She smiled big. "Now it sounds right!"

Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya gave Jaxson a job. "Count the mats for me," she said. Jaxson touched each mat. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten mats for ten kids. Everyone sat down. Finley patted the mat next to him.

Story time finished. Jaxson gave back his mat. "One," he said, putting it on the pile. He waved to Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya. "Ten tomorrow?" he asked. She laughed and said, "Ten tomorrow."

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Jackson sat at the dinner table. He had ten green beans on his plate. He wanted to count them all by himself.

He touched a bean. "One," he said. He touched the next one. "Two." His mom smiled and waited. "Three, four, five." The beans were round and little. "Six, seven, eight, nine." One bean was left. "Ten!" Jackson clapped his hands.

Then Jackson wanted to write the number ten. He had a paper and a crayon. He wrote a big 4 first. No, that was four. He rubbed it out. He drew a huge 7. No, that was seven. He looked at his mom.

"Ten is written with two numbers," she said. "A 1 and then a 0." Jackson drew a small 1. Then he drew a round 0 right after it. He held up the paper. "Ten!" he said.

At school the next day, his friend Zaya was counting sheep on a card. "One, two, three," she said. Jackson sat next to her. He wrote 1 and then 0 on his paper. "That means ten sheep," he said. Zaya counted the last sheep and laughed. "Ten!"

story:
Nora wanted to play the flower fairy game with Wren and Mivaan. The rules were simple. You pick a flower card. You hop two hops. Then you send your fairy to the flower house.

Nora picked a card. She hopped four hops. She zoomed straight to the flower house. "I win!" she said.

Wren put down her card. "That is not the game," she said. Mivaan folded his arms. He sat down on the smooth rug. Nobody hopped. Nobody picked a card.

She picked a new card. She hopped two hops. She sent her fairy to the flower house. Wren clapped. Mivaan jumped up and picked his card. All three fairies sat in the flower house together. "Now we all win," said Wren.

story:
Ryan woke up early. He found his toy monkeys on the rug. "Five monkeys for my song," he said. He set them on his bed.

Ryan sang, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed. One fell off and bumped his head!" He pushed one monkey off the bed. It fell on the rug. Now he counted. "One, two, three, four. Four monkeys left!"

Mack came over to play. "Where are the monkeys?" he asked. Ryan pointed at the rug. "They all fell off. Want to put them back?" Mack put five monkeys on the bed. "Sing it again," said Mack. "One, two, three, four, five. Ready?" Ryan smiled. "Ready!"

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Ivy sat on her bedroom floor. She had paper and a fat red crayon. She wanted to write a note for Grandpa. Grandpa was coming today.

Ivy made letters. She made them big and small. She made them all in one long line. The letters were squished together like peas in a pod. She held up the paper. "Look, a note!" she said. Then she put it on the bed for Grandpa.

Mom came in. She picked up the note. She turned it upside down. She looked and looked. "Hmm," said Mom. "My eyes feel weak today. I cannot find the words." Mom tapped her toe, thinking. Then she smiled. "Ivy, there is a space between one word and the next." She showed Ivy with two fingers. A little gap. Like that.

Ivy tried again. She wrote a word. She left a gap. She wrote the next word. Gap, word, gap, word. "Dear Grandpa, let us play," the note said now. She did not forget the gaps at all. She ran and put the note by the door, face up, so Grandpa would see it first.

The door opened. Grandpa came in. He picked up the paper. He read it right away. "Dear Grandpa, let us play," he said out loud. He laughed a big laugh. Ivy jumped up and down. "You read my words!" she said. Grandpa held out his hand. "Come on," he said. "Let us play."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Edouard loved basketball day in the school gymnasium. His team was the Blue Foxes. His friends Khalid and Abir were on the team too. But Edouard had a problem. The ball never went in. He threw it high. It hit the wall. He threw it low. It rolled away. "The hoop is playing tricks on me," he said.

Mr. Do blew his whistle. "Watch Abir," he said. Abir held the ball up. She bent her knees. She let it fly. Swish! The ball went through the hoop. The scoreboard changed. Two points! A shy boy on the bench whispered, "That's how our team scores." Edouard opened his eyes wide. The ball had to go through the hoop.

Edouard tried again. He bent his knees like Abir. He aimed up. The ball sailed through the net. "I did it!" he shouted. Khalid laughed and gave him a high five. Mr. Do clapped. After the game, they helped clean the floor. Edouard put the ball in the bag. "Same time next week?" said Abir. Edouard grinned. "Yes! I want more hoops!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Penelope ran out to the playground. The sun was big and bright. "Sunny today!" said Dax. Penelope looked up. The sun made her eyes go small. She could not see the slide. She held Emmitt's hand tight.

"Why are my eyes squinting?" she asked. Ms. Sokolov smiled. "Try a sun hat," she said. She got a blue hat. Penelope put it on. The hat made shade over her face. Now her eyes opened wide. She could see the whole slide. She could see Dax waving. She could see the swing.

It was windy too. The wind blew Emmitt's scarf. It flapped like a tail. "Your scarf looks funny," said Penelope. Emmitt laughed and held it.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain came down. Rain was not scary. Ms. Sokolov opened umbrellas. "Rainy days need umbrellas," she said. They walked inside. Penelope kept her hat on. "My hat helps in the sun," she said. "I want to wear it again tomorrow." Dax said, "Me too!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Juliette sat at the dinner table. Her bowl was full of warm soup. "One more bite," said Dad. Juliette took a big bite. Yum.

"I want to stay up late," said Juliette. "I want to play with my blocks." Dad said, "Okay, a little late." Juliette played and played. She did not sleep much.

The next morning, Dakota came over. They ran out to the yard. Juliette tried to run fast. Her legs felt slow. Her eyes felt heavy. She sat down on the grass near the swing. "I am too tired," she said.

That night, Juliette ate her dinner. She had a bath. She put on her soft pajamas. Then she said, "I will go to sleep now. Sleeping at night gives my body rest for the next day."

She slept and slept. In the morning, Dakota came again. Juliette ran fast in the yard. Her legs felt strong. "My rest worked!" she said. Dakota laughed, and they ran to the swing together.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Hudson sat in a big chair. It went up, up, up. Ms. Chanthavong put a cape on him. It was soft and it fit just right. "Time for your first haircut," she said.

Hudson's dad stood close by. Ms. Chanthavong picked up her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down. Some landed on Hudson's neck. Hudson began to wiggle. He scratched his neck with his hand.

"Why are you wiggling?" Ms. Chanthavong asked. "My neck feels itchy," Hudson said. She smiled and picked up a soft brush. She brushed the little hairs away, tick tick tick. The itchy feeling went away too. Hudson sat very still. "Where did the hairs go?" he asked. "Into my brush," she said. She tapped it over a bin. The bin was empty, and now tiny hairs fell inside.

Snip, snip, snip went the scissors. When a hair landed on his neck, Hudson said, "Itchy!" Ms. Chanthavong brushed it off right away. Then the haircut was all done. Hudson looked in the mirror. "I see a big boy," he said. Dad gave him a thumbs up, and Hudson grinned all the way home.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Eva went to Zeke's house. Zeke's mom put on a song. It had a bumpy, jumpy beat. Eva wanted to sing "Twinkle, Twinkle" with Zeke and clap too.

Eva clapped whenever she liked. Clap! Clap! Clap! Zeke shook his head. "You are clapping too fast," he said. "It sounds all mixed up." Eva got upset. Her claps and the song did not match. It was like a dream where her feet ran the wrong way.

"Listen first," said Zeke. "The song goes boom, boom, boom. Clap at the same time as the boom." They stood still and listened. Boom, boom, boom. Eva waited. Then she clapped on the boom. Clap, clap, clap. Her claps landed right on the song! She felt her hands find the music like a friend holding hands.

Then they sang. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Eva sang it all by herself. She did not miss one word. Zeke clapped along with her singing. Eva laughed and clapped too, right on the beat, all the way to "what you are."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Evan went to the library with his friend Kacey. Mr. Kerr had a big box of new books. "One book each," said Mr. Kerr. Evan picked a book about trucks. Kacey picked a book about a bear.

Kacey read fast. Soon she wanted Evan's truck book too. Evan held it close. Then he looked at her book. The bear had a big, wide yawn. Evan wanted to see it. "You read mine," said Evan. "I read yours." They swapped books. That worked well.

At the desk, Mr. Kerr stamped Evan's book. Evan took it and ran to the door. Kacey stopped him. "Wait," she said. "What do we say?" Evan thought hard. He ran back to the desk. "Thank you, Mr. Kerr," he said. Mr. Kerr smiled a big smile.

"Thank you too," said Mr. Kerr. "For remembering." Evan gave his book a little kiss and hugged it tight.

"Can we cook pretend soup with the bear book?" Kacey asked. Evan laughed all the way to the car.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Milan ran to the big tire swing at the playground. His friend Liam was already there. "Let's play rocket ship," said Liam. Milan wanted to be the rocket ship. But he did not know how to start it.

Liam held the tire with both hands. "Watch me," he said. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Liam jumped high on "blast off." The tire swing swung back and forth. Milan clapped his hands.

"My turn," said Milan. He got in the tire and held on tight. The tire felt bumpy under his tummy. Liam counted, "Ten, nine, eight, seven." Milan giggled. "Six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Milan jumped up and the swing went whoosh.

Ms. Thompson was sitting on a bench. "That is called a countdown," she said. "You counted backward from ten down to one." Milan smiled a big smile. His fuzzy hair blew in the wind. "Again!" said Milan. Liam laughed. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Kinsley ran into the big room at the cultural center. There were rows and rows of little clay cups. Her mom held a box of them. "Can I help?" Kinsley asked. "Yes," Mom said. "Put them in a long row."

Kinsley set out the little cups one by one. She counted them as she went. Her friend Ryder came to help too. He put wicks in each cup. Then a grown-up poured oil into them.

"What are these called?" Kinsley asked. Mom said, "They are called diyas." Ryder rolled a diya across the table to Kinsley. She laughed and set it back in the row.

Soon Mr. Kelly came with a small flame. He touched it to the first wick. A little light popped up. Then he lit the next one, and the next. Kinsley watched from far back, where it was safe.

The whole row glowed now. One little cup had made one little light. Then all the little lights made a big bright line. "Look, Ryder!" Kinsley said. "They all shine together!" The diyas blinked like tiny stars on the table.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Emma put on her swim class suit. It had little ducks on it. Her mom took her to the big hotel pool.

Emma hoped she could swim today. Her class was by the steps. Mr. Bui was the teacher. "Hello, Emma," he said. "We will kick and blow bubbles."

Chelsea ran fast to the pool. "Wait," said Mr. Bui. "The floor is wet. Wet floors are slippery. Walk, please." Chelsea stopped her feet. She walked very slow, like a turtle. Emma laughed. "Slow turtle feet," she said.

Emma got in the water. She held the rail. She kicked and kicked. She blew ten bubbles. Then she let go. She kicked all by herself. "Look at me!" she called.

After class, Emma felt fresh and clean. She walked, not ran, to her towel. Chelsea walked too, turtle style. "See you next time," said Mr. Bui. Emma waved and waved.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Xavier waited by the gate. Ms. Grewal called the names. "Yunus! Neo! Xavier!" Xavier ran to his dad.

At home, Dad said, "First we wash hands. Then we eat." Xavier looked at the soap. It felt smooth. He rubbed it. Nothing happened. "Where are the bubbles?" he asked.

Dad turned on the tap. Water ran cool and fast. Xavier held his hands under it. He rubbed the soap again. Bubbles! Lots of soft, white bubbles covered his fingers.

"Look, Dad! Bubbles!" Xavier piled them on his chin. "I have a beard!" Yunus made one too, at school. Xavier giggled and giggled.

He washed the bubbles off. His hands were clean and shiny. Then he ate his lunch. After that came a bath, with more bubbles. Then he would wear his soft pajamas with the little animal on the front.

"Soap and water," said Xavier. "Bubbles every time."

He rubbed his soapy tummy and blew one bubble off his hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story: Scarlett was awake early. She wanted to wash her face all by herself. Dad put a small ice cube in her cup of water. Scarlett picked up the ice cube with her fingers. It felt so cold! She dropped it into the cup fast. Plop! Her ears heard the little splash. Then she washed her hands with warm, soapy water. The soap smelled like strawberries. She touched the soft towel to dry off. Dad held out his hand. "Here is your toothpaste," he said. It tasted like mint on her tongue. Scarlett looked in the mirror. Her eyes saw the ice cube floating in the cup. She touched it once more, very quick. Still cold! She laughed and poked it with her toothbrush. "Brrr," she said, and waved at the girl in the mirror.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Ayla went to the store with her mama. She held the shopping list. The list was small. The cart was big.

Ayla saw Ms. Do in the store. "Hello, Ayla," said Ms. Do. Ms. Do was buying soup. The soup can was cold from the shelf. Mama picked a warm loaf of bread. "Hot and cold," said Ms. Do with a smile.

Then Ayla saw it. A toy drum sat on a shelf. It was red and round. "Can we get it?" asked Ayla. Mama said yes. Ayla tapped the drum. BANG! It was so loud. A man by the bread put his hands over his ears. A baby began to cry. Ayla made her hands go fast on the drum. Loud, loud, loud.

Ayla stopped. She made one small, slow tap. Tap. That was quiet. The baby stopped crying. The man took his hands down. "Loud and quiet are opposites," said Ms. Do. Ayla tapped loud. Then she tapped quiet. One drum, two sounds!

A cart rolled by, fast. A old man walked by, slow. A box began to drop from a shelf. A worker caught it. He put it back in a tidy line.

At home, Ayla played her drum. She tapped quiet like a little rain. Then she tapped loud like a big storm. Mama laughed. "Play your quiet rain for me," she said. Ayla tapped, tap, tap, tap, soft as a spring day.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Arya sat on the rug at school. Amari had a shiny red kite. It had a long tail. Arya wanted to hold it very much.

She reached out her hand. Then she stopped. She looked at Amari's face. She put her hand in her lap. "May I have a turn?" she asked.

Amari smiled big. "Yes! You said may I!" He put the kite in her hands. Arya felt the string. It was smooth and long. "Thank you," she said.

Jose ran over too. He grabbed for the tail. "No, no," said Ms. Sinclair softly. "Try asking, Jose."

Jose thought for a moment. "May I hold the tail?" he said. "Yes, you may," said Arya. She held the kite safe and snug. Jose held the tail. They walked round and round the rug, humming a little song. "Zoom goes the kite!" said Amari, pushing it through the air.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Evelyn sat on the rug at home. Her blocks were all around her. She wanted to give her best block a sticker on every side. But she did not know how many sides it had.

First she looked at her snack. Her cookie was a circle. It was round like a ball. She stuck out her tongue and licked a crumb from her lip. Then she put the cookie down and looked at the block.

"One," said Evelyn. She put a red sticker on a flat side. The side was a square. She turned the block over. "Two." She put a blue sticker there. That side was a square too. "Three, four, five." A sticker went on each flat face. Her socks were stinky, so she wiggled her toes and kept going. She turned the block one more time. "Six." The last sticker was yellow.

"Mom, how many sides does a block have?" Evelyn asked. Mom came to look. "Count your stickers," said Mom. Evelyn lifted the block up high. "One, two, three, four, five, six," she said. Six stickers. Six flat faces. Each one was a square, just like her red sticker.

Evelyn held the block to the window. The sunlight made six shiny squares glow. "Six," she said again, and gave the block a hug.
